title: Dark matter needs 276 parameters to fit 138 galaxies; this physicist uses 4
dek: Dark matter theory assigns each galaxy two free halo parameters you must back-calculate from measured rotation curves; Mannheim argues the universal laws naturally embedded in rotation data represent what Newton's gold standard truly demands.
why: If you want to understand where the dark matter crisis bottlenecks and how conformal gravity derives Einstein's equations starting from Newton, this is the most complete derivation currently available.
who: Physicists and physics enthusiasts interested in dark matter alternatives and complete derivations of general relativity.
skip: If you're already familiar with general relativity, you can skip the section from 1:33:00 to 2:05:00 covering step-by-step derivations of metrics, geodesics, and Riemann tensors.

points.h: Dark energy prediction may be physics' worst fit by orders of magnitude
points.body: The cosmological constant problem is a century old. Using the weak interaction scale, Omega Lambda should be on the order of 10^60; using Planck scale, 10^120. Yet observations never support values exceeding roughly 0.7. If these estimates are correct, Mannheim notes, all cosmic microwave background fits would be wrong by 60 to 120 orders of magnitude—arguably the worst fit in physics history. This is why Mannheim treats dark matter, dark energy, and quantum gravity as stemming from one mistake: inappropriately extending Newton's and Einstein's theories beyond the solar system.

points.h: Dark matter's one success and one failure both occurred in the solar system
points.body: When Uranus's orbit deviated from expectations, astronomers hypothesized an unseen planet (what today we'd call dark matter) perturbing it—and found Neptune. This is dark matter theory's only documented success. Apply the same logic to Mercury: an invisible planet called Vulcan pulling at it. But the solar system's inner region is too thoroughly mapped; Vulcan was ruled out definitively. This marks dark matter theory's first documented failure. Mercury's orbital anomaly was ultimately explained not by an invisible body, but by Einstein's correction to Newton's law itself.

points.h: Dwarf galaxies revealed dark matter's core assumptions weren't universal
points.body: Bright spiral galaxies show a dark matter to luminous matter ratio of roughly 3:1 or 4:1; dwarf galaxies reach 8:1 or 9:1—more than double. The halo parameters are not universal constants; they must be tuned per galaxy. More significantly: in bright spirals, Newton's law holds perfectly in inner regions with anomalies only outside; in dwarf galaxies, Newton's law breaks down even in inner regions. This suggests dwarf galaxies present the harder problem, not the outer flat rotation curve.

points.h: Four parameters fit 4,000 data points; dark matter requires 276
points.body: Mannheim and James O'Brien used four universal constants—beta star, gamma star, gamma zero, kappa—to fit rotation curves from 138 galaxies covering approximately 4,000 data points, using only visible mass. Dark matter theory, by contrast, needs two independent parameters per galaxy halo (like rho zero and r zero in isothermal models), totaling 276 for 138 galaxies; these must be reverse-engineered from measured rotation speeds. Dark matter doesn't know what values each galaxy needs; the galaxies themselves "know."

points.h: Fourth-order Poisson equation makes local systems sense cosmic-scale matter
points.body: Newtonian gravity obeys a famous theorem: matter outside a spherically symmetric distribution exerts no net force inside, since gravitational force falls as one over R squared while solid angle grows as R squared, perfectly canceling. This is gravity's locality. Replace the equation with a fourth-order one, and solutions contain a potential growing linearly with distance. Farther matter contributes ever stronger potential; local dynamics inevitably sense cosmic-scale mass distribution. Mannheim calls this true Mach's principle: not through some mysterious mechanism of inertial frames, but through the potential's failure to decay with distance.

points.h: Seven-year-old prediction confirmed by 2025 data at ten orders of magnitude lower
points.body: In 2018, Mannheim predicted that the radial acceleration relation, in the extreme low-acceleration limit, would have V squared divided by R approach a constant (gamma zero), not continue bending as MOND or McGaugh's formula does. Data released in 2025 extended observations from 10^-12 down to 10^-14 acceleration units and converged around 10^-11—exactly conformal gravity's 2018 prediction value. Newton's curve and MOND curve both fail to match this new data.

points.h: Einstein's equation was born assuming Newton holds at all scales
points.body: Einstein's field equations directly generalize Newton's Poisson equation, which means accepting them implicitly extends Newton's gravity to all non-relativistic scales at any distance—including galaxies and galaxy clusters, scales never truly tested before. Mannheim identifies this as the dark matter problem's root: use these equations and you're forced to invoke dark matter to close the gap; the only escape is to retain geodesics and the equivalence principle while replacing the metric-determining equation, provided it still respects general coordinate invariance.

points.h: Schwarzschild was tested; Einstein's equation was never proven unique
points.body: Eddington noted in 1922 that any theory whose action rests on higher Ricci scalar powers still yields Ricci-flat vacuum solutions, preserving Schwarzschild validity—these are quadratic gravity theories. That means all classical solar system tests (light bending, gravitational redshift, Mercury's precession) only verified that spacetime outside the Sun is Ricci-flat; they never verified Einstein's equation is the unique solution satisfying this condition. This is why Mannheim pursues conformal invariance to generalize Schwarzschild rather than the Poisson equation.
